title: Co-op Programs in Canada: Work Placements, Tuition Planning and Career Value

runs.t: A co-operative education (co-op) programme combines academic study with structured, supervised work placements related to a student’s field. For international students, a co-op can provide Canadian workplace experience, professional contacts and a chance to test a career path. It should not be treated as guaranteed employment or as a reliable way to fund the full cost of tuition.

Compare the programme’s placement structure, employer network, placement eligibility, work-term schedule, tuition and fees, and historical placement outcomes. From 1 April 2026, post-secondary international students no longer need a separate co-op work permit for qualifying work placements that are required by and approved as part of their programme. The placement must still meet the immigration and institutional conditions.

sections.title: What makes a programme a co-op?

runs.t: A formal co-op usually alternates academic terms with paid or unpaid work terms. A qualifying student work placement must be required to complete the study programme and approved by the designated learning institution. Placements can include co-op terms, internships, practicums and other approved work-integrated learning experiences.

Not every internship advertised by a university is a mandatory programme placement. Optional work, an independently sourced job or a placement that is not part of the approved curriculum may be treated differently for immigration purposes.

IRCC states that, as of 1 April 2026, post-secondary international students do not need a separate co-op work permit for student work placements such as co-ops or internships, where the placement is required by the programme and approved by the DLI. Secondary students still need a co-op work permit. Students must continue to meet the conditions of their study permit and their institution’s placement requirements.

IRCC also states that student work placements have no weekly hour limit under this placement rule, but the placement cannot total more than 50% of the study programme. This is distinct from ordinary off-campus employment during academic terms, which is generally limited to 24 hours per week for eligible students.

rows.t: Part of the approved academic programme and required to complete it.
Must be approved by the DLI and meet IRCC placement conditions.
Student and employer must ensure the student meets off-campus work conditions.
No weekly limit under the qualifying placement rule; total placement cannot exceed 50% of programme.
Up to 24 hours per week during regular academic sessions; unlimited during scheduled breaks if eligible.
Usually related to the field of study and may include structured learning objectives.
May be unrelated to the course.
May be paid or unpaid, depending on programme and employer.
Usually paid, subject to applicable employment law.

sections.title: How to assess a college or university co-op programme

runs.t: Is co-op compulsory, optional or simply an internship support service?
How many work terms are included, and how long is each term?
Does the institution arrange placements, provide a job board or expect students to secure their own role?
What percentage of eligible students obtained a placement in the latest published cohort?
Are placement rates calculated only for students actively seeking a role, or for the entire class?
Which employers and sectors recruited recently, and are those examples current?
Are international students eligible for all advertised placements?
What happens if a student does not secure a placement—does the programme extend, change or require an alternative course?
Are there additional co-op fees, insurance requirements or travel costs?

sections.title: Earnings: model a range, not a promise

runs.t: Co-op earnings vary by occupation, employer, location, experience, work-term length and market conditions.

It should show conservative, middle and optimistic scenarios and allow the student to enter their own offer details. Clearly label any wage figure as an assumption or cite a current employer or institutional dataset.

Co-op experience can help a graduate develop skills and professional contacts, but a co-op placement does not automatically create permanent-residence points or count as qualifying work experience for a federal immigration programme. For example, work performed while a person was a full-time student is generally not counted toward the Canadian Experience Class minimum work-experience requirement. Graduates must assess the exact federal and provincial rules applicable to their later employment.

Do not market a co-op as a direct PR pathway. Its value is primarily educational and career-related. Any immigration benefit depends on the graduate’s later eligibility, work authorisation, occupation, experience, language and the rules in force at that time.

sections.title: Questions to ask before paying a deposit

runs.t: Is the co-op component written into the programme structure and letter of offer?
Is the placement mandatory for graduation, and how is it approved?
What are the latest placement outcomes, with the cohort and calculation method disclosed?
Which employers recruited in the last two terms, and for what roles?
What support is available for CVs, interviews, networking and work authorisation?
What is the academic plan if a placement is not secured?
What is the total programme cost including co-op fees, travel and possible extra terms?

faq.q: Do international students need a co-op work permit in 2026?

runs.t: For qualifying post-secondary work placements required by and approved as part of the programme, a separate co-op work permit is no longer required from 1 April 2026. Secondary students still need one.

faq.q: Can I work unlimited hours in a co-op placement?

runs.t: The qualifying placement rule has no weekly hour limit, but the placement cannot total more than 50% of the study programme. Ordinary off-campus work remains subject to its own limits.
No. Payment depends on the programme, employer and placement. Check the institution’s current terms and outcomes.

faq.q: Does co-op work count for Canadian PR?

runs.t: Do not assume it does. Work completed while a full-time student is generally not counted toward CEC minimum work experience. Later qualifying employment must be assessed under the rules in force.

faq.q: Will a college guarantee a co-op job?

runs.t: A programme may provide placement support, but students should not assume a guaranteed job unless the institution’s written terms clearly say so. Verify placement rates and what happens if no placement is secured.
